newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Tietmeyer's EMU view poses huge political challenge.
newsitem.headline: Tietmeyer's EMU view poses huge political challenge.

text.p: German Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer's warning on durable economic convergence for those wishing to join a single European currency exposes a deep-seated worry over a monetary union with too many members.

EU monetary officials and analysts say Tietmeyer's comments on Monday exemplify the Bundesbank's long-held belief that economic and monetary union (EMU) would work best with countries which have a culture of stability rooted in society.

"It is a question of durability and sustainability," Tietmeyer told a Bonn conference. "It is important in the selection (of EMU participants) that the member countries do not just reach the criteria through a breathless short-term effort."

Experts say his views, however, pose a problem, not only for countries such as Italy, Spain and Portugal, which are knocking harder and harder on EMU's door, but for those within Europe's political mainstream.

"I think at some stage this will become a question of politics at the highest level," said one senior EU monetary official, adding that Tietmeyer's remarks were clearly designed to refer to the recent budget plans of southern European states.

The dilemma such a position poses is twofold. EMU is very much seen as an key step in advancing political integration across a broad array of areas. Such an objective argues for it to start with the largest possible number of states possible.
Too narrow a group could expose the 15-nation bloc to unforeseen and unwelcome political rifts as they struggle with tough issues such as enlargement and a common foreign policy.

But the risk of spreading the EMU net as wide as possible, is precisely the one Tietmeyer refers to -- a perception, particularly in the financial markets, of a project cobbled together for largely political motives.
Such views could undermine the all important credibility EMU needs if it is to ultimately succeed.

"Tietmeyer's fear is that such countries (Italy and Spain) would achieve in one year the necessary conditions and diverge again. They might prove a danger for the durability of monetary union," added another official.
Bruce Kasman, senior economist at J.P. Morgan in London, says he cannot envisage a situation where countries are kept out of EMU simply if there are doubts about their long-term fitness.
"I don't see how the EMU group can leave out a country that meets the criteria," he said, likening such a debate to Germany's negotiations on the economic terms of reunificiation.

At the time, there was fierce resistance from the Bundesbank to Chancellor Helmut Kohl's proposal to swap the West German mark one-for-one with East German marks. Such an exchange was seen as detrimental to the long-run economic health of the eastern half of country.

Kohl eventually won the argument, but there are still questions over whether the choice was the best one on economic grounds. Many observers say Kohl's brilliance was in seeing the broader political implications of such a decision.

Tietmeyer's position is clearly at odds with those in Bonn and no one quite knows how the two will be reconciled, say analysts. "This is a signal of tensions within the German establishment, notes Kasman.
One option might be to give countries like Italy a clear and definitive timetable on when they might join EMU so as to minimise the political fallout.

"If the countries confirm their (economic) performance they would join the first group without much dealy," says one official. Such a decision could be made late in 1997, when a good idea of the year's economic performance is available.
